title: The Master and the Centrão — Eddie Would Go
units: Brazil · Corruption · Politics · Financial System · 22 min read
The Master and the Centrão
How the collapse of Banco Master exposed the architecture of Brazilian state capture and threw the country into a war between its three branches of government, five months before the elections.
Brasília · 10 May 2026 · Brazil · Corruption · Politics
«O Centrão vive do acesso ao Estado, não de um programa político.»
— Marcos Nobre, Brazilian philosopher and political scientist.

On the night of 17 November 2024, Daniel Bueno Vorcaro tried to board a private jet at Congonhas airport in São Paulo, bound for Dubai. The Federal Police were waiting for him on the tarmac. On his phones — eight in all, some hidden in compartments in his luggage — was something more valuable than the messages of a banker on the run. There was the draft of a law written in the offices of Banco Master. Records of monthly transfers to relatives of senators. And there was, according to the Federal Police, proof that the difference between politics and business in Brazil is not a line but a fiction.

This is Brazil's most significant corruption case since Lava Jato. But Operation Compliance Zero, which is investigating the collapse of Banco Master and its political ramifications, is something qualitatively different from that scandal of a decade ago. Lava Jato was about the capture of public contracts. This is about the capture of legislation itself.

The combined financial hole of Master and Will Bank — its subsidiary — liquidated in November 2025 and January 2026 respectively, approaches R$47 billion (around US$9.5 billion). It is the largest banking failure in Brazil's recent history. But the number that matters most politically is not that one. It is the one describing what almost happened before the collapse. And the number that will matter most in October — the distance between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro in the polls — is not in that case file either. It is in an audio message sent the night before Vorcaro's arrest.
I. The Amendment That Should Not Have Existed

In August 2024, Senator Ciro Nogueira — national president of the Progressistas Party (PP), former Chief of Staff in the Bolsonaro government and one of the architects of the Centrão for two decades — tabled a proposed amendment to PEC 65/2023. The text sought to widen the coverage of the Credit Guarantee Fund (FGC), Brazil's deposit insurance scheme, from R$250,000 to R$1 million per depositor.

The effect of that widening would have been, according to Federal Police investigators, to sextuple Banco Master's capacity to raise funds. Vorcaro had built his business selling CDBs — deposit certificates with yields far above the market — to thousands of retail investors, many of them drawn by the FGC's umbrella. If the guarantee limit rose fourfold, the universe of clients who could enter the scheme multiplied in the same way.

What the agents found on Vorcaro's phones left no room for ambiguity. The draft of the amendment was written inside the bank. A sealed envelope containing the exact text was delivered to Nogueira's residence. The senator tabled it verbatim in the Senate. "It came out exactly as I sent it", Vorcaro wrote to his partners after the bill was filed, according to the Federal Police report to the Supreme Federal Court.

The amendment did not prosper. But its existence reveals something more disturbing than the bribe itself: the naturalness with which the legal text was subcontracted to the private sector. There was no drafting in a technical committee, no consultation with regulators, none of the steps that in theory separate particular interest from public norm. Just an envelope.
II. The Architect of the Centrão

To understand why the arrest of Ciro Nogueira — carried out on 7 May 2026, in the fifth phase of Operation Compliance Zero — is an event of another dimension, it is necessary to understand what the Centrão is and why Nogueira has been its most representative figure of the last fifteen years.

The Centrão is neither a party nor an ideology. It is an infrastructure. It is the set of parties — PP, União Brasil, MDB, Republicanos and others — that guarantee parliamentary majorities in exchange for negotiated access to the public budget, posts in the executive and a zone of protection from judicial investigation. Lula used it. Bolsonaro used it. Dilma tried to do without it and it cost her the presidency.

Nogueira was not merely a member of the Centrão. He was, as one analyst in Brasília described him, "the one who knew the price of everything". Chief of Staff between 2021 and 2022, he coordinated Bolsonaro's legislative agenda in Congress with an efficiency many in the government admired without saying so in public. His capacity to move votes was real and his network of loyalties cut across parties, states and mandates.

The Federal Police describe a scheme investigators call an "arranjo funcional orientado por benefício mútuo" — a functional arrangement oriented by mutual benefit. The money did not circulate in envelopes: it was channelled through monthly payments to companies linked to the senator's family, shareholdings acquired at a fraction of their real value, and the systematic use of Vorcaro's assets — properties, aircraft, luxury hotels in New York. The image that condenses the link: the two seated side by side on a panel at a business forum in Rome, months before the Federal Police detained the banker on the tarmac at Congonhas.
III. The State Bank, the Banker and the Apartments

Before the fifth phase of the anti-corruption operation targeted the Centrão, the fourth — executed on 16 April — had revealed another vector of the scheme: the Bank of Brasília (BRB), a publicly owned institution controlled by the government of the Federal District.

Paulo Henrique Costa, former president of the BRB, was arrested that day and taken to Papuda prison. The order from STF Justice André Mendonça accused him of having negotiated R$146.5 million in bribes with Vorcaro, materialised in six luxury apartments distributed between São Paulo and Brasília, with R$74 million in property transfers already traced. This is not an inventory of stolen goods. It is evidence that the covert bailout mechanism had a price agreed in advance, paid in bricks and mortar.

The BRB, under Costa's management, had acquired credit portfolios from Master at amounts the authorities describe as artificially inflated. The operation functioned as a covert liquidity line: the public bank bought assets from the private one at prices the market would not have validated, effectively transferring the risk of Vorcaro's Ponzi scheme to the public balance sheet. Structurally, it is the first time in Brazil that a state-controlled institution has been used as a liquidity rescue vehicle for a bankrupt private bank. There was no precedent.
IV. Tether and the Global Geometry of the Scandal

The most unexpected dimension of the case was brought on 7 May by Tether — the issuer of USDT, the stablecoin with more than US$140 billion in circulation and the most widely used liquidity instrument in the global crypto ecosystem. The company filed suit in a São Paulo court to recover R$1.6 billion linked to a US$300 million loan extended to an entity of the Master group. With that move, Tether ceased to be an international observer and became a creditor in the largest bank fraud case in Brazil's recent history.

To understand why Tether was in that position, one has to understand its institutional moment. The company has spent years trying to dispel doubts about its reserves and business model with a legitimation strategy along a clear axis: building relationships with regulated banks in emerging markets that would give it access to real flows and jurisdictional presence. Brazil — with its crypto market among the five largest in the world and Pix as a mass instant payments infrastructure — was a logical destination. Master, a fast-growing bank operating at the margins of conventional due diligence, was the sort of counterparty such a strategy attracts.

The mechanics of the loan reveal the structural risk. By 2024, Banco Master had a problem the formal market was beginning to detect: its CDBs paid yields no sustainable model could justify, and the regulator was starting to ask questions. Traditional credit was tightening. Tether, without the capital and compliance restrictions of a regulated bank, extended the liquidity the formal system had stopped providing. The insolvent bank used the stablecoin to buy time. The stablecoin used the bank to gain presence in a strategic market. When the scheme collapsed, Tether discovered that its counterparty was not a fintech in difficulty but the centre of an investigation into systematic fraud and legislative capture.

The pattern has direct antecedents. In 2023, Tether had exposure to Silvergate and Signature Bank before their collapses in the American crypto-banking crisis. In each case the logic was the same: the stablecoin issuer offers liquidity without the restrictions of the formal system; the bank offers legitimacy and real flows. The alliance works while the bank works. When it fails, the decentralised finance narrative dissolves and the stablecoin issuer appears queuing in a courtroom alongside all the other creditors.

What the Master Case adds is not just another example of the pattern. It is confirmation that crypto-banking integration can amplify fraud risk in emerging markets, not merely absorb it. A bank that uses stablecoins to extend its runway has access to liquidity that is opaque, fast and of limited traceability for the local regulator. That is no accident of design. When that functionality is documented in a Brazilian court file, the global discussion about how to regulate crypto-banking integration has a case study that no argument about financial innovation can ignore.
V. The War of the Three Branches

In Brasília, no political event is read in a single dimension. The fifth phase of Compliance Zero came eight days after the Senate, led by Davi Alcolumbre, rejected the nomination of Jorge Messias to the STF — an unprecedented result in 132 years of Brazilian constitutional history.

Justice André Mendonça, who had publicly called Messias his "brother" and was the principal champion of his entry to the court, is the same judge who authorised the warrants against Nogueira — Alcolumbre's closest ally in the Senate. The reading in the corridors of Congress was instantaneous and unanimous: Compliance Zero had become the definitive weapon in a war of survival between the Supreme Court and the Legislature.

The map of factions inside the STF is, in this context, as relevant as the legal case itself. According to Brazilian press sources, the court today operates in at least three blocs: that of Justice Alexandre de Moraes, with Gilmar Mendes, Flávio Dino and on occasion Dias Toffoli, all with solid lines of communication to Alcolumbre; that of Mendonça, with Kassio Nunes Marques and Luiz Fux, who lean to the juridical right; and a third, more institutional one — Fachin, Cristiano Zanin, Cármen Lúcia — with traffic in both camps.

The dimension that complicates the "judicial holy war" narrative is that Moraes's bloc is not untouched by the scandal. His wife, the lawyer Viviane Barci de Moraes, has a R$129 million three-year contract with Banco Master and the use of aircraft belonging to a company of the former banker Vorcaro. Toffoli, for his part, declared himself "suspect" and recused himself from voting in the case. The result is a judicial system in which the arbiters of the scandal have their own exposures to it.
The court today operates as three blocs watching one another. All have something to lose. All have something to hide.
VI. The Electoral Impact and the Flávio Problem

For Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of the convicted former president, the Master Case arrived at the worst possible moment. His strategy of building an opposition coalition — PL, PP and União Brasil — depended on Nogueira as the articulating piece. Now that piece is under electronic monitoring and his allies in the PP are trying to distance themselves. On 9 May, in Santa Catarina, Flávio declared that the Nogueira case was "serious" but that the investigation was legitimate. "He is lucky to have as rapporteur someone serious, André Mendonça", he said — a sentence that simultaneously defends the ally, praises the judge and implicitly fires at the process that convicted his father. Few sentences have concentrated so much geometry in recent Brazilian politics.

Three days later, on 13 May, the situation changed dimension. The Intercept Brasil published audio, messages and bank receipts proving something Flávio had emphatically denied in public: a direct and close relationship with Daniel Vorcaro. The senator had negotiated with the banker a financing package of US$24 million — equivalent to R$134 million — to produce Dark Horse, a biographical film about the life of his father Jair Bolsonaro, directed by Cyrus Nowrasteh and starring Jim Caviezel. At least US$10.6 million — some R$61 million — was actually transferred between February and May 2025 in six operations, to the Havengate Development Fund LP, based in Texas.

The audio published by The Intercept was unequivocal. In it, Flávio called Vorcaro "brother" and asked him to unblock overdue payments to avoid an international scandal. A day before the banker's arrest at Congonhas — on 16 November 2024 — Flávio had written to him: "Irmão, estou e estarei contigo sempre, não tem meia conversa entre a gente." The banker was arrested the following day.

Flávio's chain of contradictions was, in itself, politically devastating. First he denied any relationship with Vorcaro. Then he denied having met him after his release with an electronic tag. When evidence of that meeting emerged, he admitted it. When the audio came out, he tried to redefine the operation as a "legitimate search for private sponsorship". The Intercept Brasil documented that he changed his version twice in a single day. The account that the money was clean and without quid pro quo was weakened by the geology of the case itself: the man financing the film is the same man under investigation for the largest bank fraud in Brazil's recent history.

The family dimension of the case expanded on 15 May, when The Intercept revealed that Eduardo Bolsonaro — the youngest son, a federal deputy stripped of his seat and based in Washington — had given direct instructions on the sending of funds to the United States linked to the Dark Horse negotiation. Messages recovered by investigators show Eduardo coordinating with an intermediary identified as Altieris Santana on the mechanisms for transferring money to Havengate. The Federal Police are investigating whether that money financed Eduardo's operating and personal expenses during his informal exile on American territory.

The electoral impact was immediate and measurable. A week before the audio, polls showed a technical tie between Flávio and Lula. After 13 May, the picture changed structurally. AtlasIntel recorded Lula moving from 47.5% to 49.1% in the first round, while Flávio fell from 47.8% to 42.6%. In a run-off, the gap widened to seven points: 48.9% against 41.8%. Datafolha confirmed the movement with an even larger difference: Lula stretched his lead from 3 to 9 points. The percentage of Brazilians who perceive Bolsonarism as linked to the Master scheme jumped from 28.3% to 43.3% within days. Flávio's head of communications resigned. Markets reacted with swings in government bonds at the prospect of a weakening of the main opposition candidate.

In Congress, the revelation triggered seven requests to open a parliamentary inquiry into the relationship between Banco Master and the Bolsonaro family. Two of those requests are in the signature-gathering phase. The installation of a joint inquiry depends on authorisation from Davi Alcolumbre — who has his own reasons for handling the calendar cautiously in an election year. The film Dark Horse, whose release had been announced for 11 September 2026 — a few weeks before the October presidential election — now has its financing under judicial investigation and its producer in prison.

In the Planalto, Lula's government abandoned its silence. If until 12 May an internal directive ordered ministers to refrain from commenting on Compliance Zero, from the 14th Lula chose direct attack. At an event in Barretos, he said before the cameras that "this hospital has no money from Vorcaro". The phrase was deliberate: useful, concise, unrepeatable. For the PT, the Master case ceased to be a transversal risk and became a lever. The Centrão, faithful to its logic of interested inertia, began to distance itself from Flávio and to explore agreements with the government. The question is no longer whether the scandal affected the campaign. It is whether it leaves Flávio enough room to recover before October.
VII. The Business Model That Was Always There

It is tempting to read the Master Case as an anomaly: an especially audacious banker, an especially extensive network, an especially sophisticated corruption. But Marco Antonio Teixeira, of the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, puts it another way: "There is no escape for any side of the political spectrum. Everyone has something to lose". What is on trial is not only Vorcaro or only Nogueira. It is the model.

The model is this: a system in which access to legislative power has a market price, in which that price is paid in instruments that can be disguised as investments or dividends, and in which the regulators who ought to prevent it have their own exposures to the same ecosystem. Lava Jato attacked physical public works. Compliance Zero is attacking the financial engineering that replaced them once that frontier became too visible.

Vorcaro, from his remand cell in São Paulo, is negotiating a plea bargain. Judge Mendonça rejected the first drafts as insufficient. In the negotiation are the names the Federal Police and the Public Prosecutor's Office do not yet have in the file but want. Those names will determine whether the sixth phase, and the seventh, reach the Planalto or stop at the Centrão. In Brasília, that question is the only one that matters this week.

Vorcaro's yacht, which appeared at the wedding of Nogueira's daughter in 2024 — reported by Bloomberg — is, in retrospect, the perfect image of an era. An ostentatious banker, a powerful politician, a family celebration. The photograph is evidence of nothing. But the metaphor is: when worlds that ought to be separate arrive at the same harbour, the question is not whether there was an agreement. It is since when.
Eddie would go. The most dangerous wave is not the one that brings down the system. It is the one that shows the system was the wave all along.
